Ben Orlin is back at it again with an [installment of Math With Bad Drawings](https://mathwithbaddrawings.com/2016/06/22/what-students-see-when-they-look-at-algebra/). This one is about how students view algebra.

<figure class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail">
<img src="https://mathwithbaddrawings.files.wordpress.com/2016/06/20160620170224_00003.jpg?w=1164" class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail" />
</figure>

Read the whole thing for context.

I don't know if it's years of experience or a literature review that produced his “cases.” I do know (and this is my experience talking) that's he's spot on.

I would add a case from precalculus that's hard for me: students struggle with the idea of *function*. Here are some bad drawings of my own.

<figure class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail">
<img src="http://svgur.com/i/6X.svg" class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail" />
</figure>

A function is a relation between two sets, which has a unique “output” for each “input.” Mathematicians tend to think of a function as a kind of machine which converts elements in one set (for instance, numbers) to elements in another.

<figure class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail">
<img src="http://svgur.com/i/7G.svg" class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail" />
</figure>

My experience with students is that a function is a graph, and $a$ and $b$ arbitrary numbers on the $x$- and $y$-axis.

<figure class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail">
<img src="http://svgur.com/i/6J.svg" class="img-responsive, img-thumbnail" />
</figure>

In general, graphs are not a bad way to think about functions, with a few caveats. One is that the independent axis is too often assumed to be “time.” It's hard to think of supply and demand depending on price when you only think of functions as depending on time.

Another is that your typical picture of a function may not be generic enough. I've drawn the graph of the function $f(x) = x^2$ because that is what most students think of when they are asked what a function is: “you know, like $x^2$.” Another student might draw a squiggle, which is more general, but still continuous. If all your mental models of functions are continuous, it's hard to work with functions that could be discontinuous. One of my grad school profs would say this over and over again: “Remember, if it's an $L^1$ function, it's **probably discontinuous everywhere**” (accompanied by wild flapping of his arms to mimic the graph of such a function).

You may point out that this image is *wrong* in that the point $(a,b)$ is not on the graph of $f$. That is, this picture does not illustrate the statement $f(a)=b$. I agree, and my point is that many students think of functions as graphs *without connecting the points on the graph to values of the function*. For these students, their one good framework is flawed.

When teaching, I try to emphasize these connections as much as possible. Functions are graphs, machines, rules, and so forth. I do “air graph” functions with my arms. Luckily in calculus most functions are piecewise $C^\infty$.
